Do the three methods differ in community composition? (Study B, Question 1)

What this document is. The first Study B question: do pill, injectable and vaginal ring users have differently composed vaginal microbiomes? This is the microbiome half of the week — the same kind of analysis as Tuesday’s ordination module, but now testing the three arms against each other. We start with a map (ordination), then a formal test of the map (PERMANOVA), then ask whether any individual species differ (DESeq2 on raw counts). Full data QC lives in 01-qc.html; this document repeats only the checks this analysis depends on.

library(tidyverse)
library(here)
library(DESeq2)
library(microViz)
library(phyloseq)
library(vegan)
library(patchwork)   # lets p_arm + p_com put two plots side by side

source(here("R/count_tables.R"))

d  <- read_counts("group_b")
sp <- d$species         # 220 species x 93 samples, RAW counts
md <- d$metadata        # one row per sample, same order as the columns

# Community type, same rule as 01-qc and notebook 02: Lactobacillus genus
# >= half of the sample's species reads. Used only to label the right-hand
# ordination panel — the tests below use arm, from the metadata.
lacto_taxa <- d$taxonomy |> filter(Genus == "Lactobacillus") |> pull(taxon)
lacto_frac <- colSums(sp[lacto_taxa, , drop = FALSE]) / colSums(sp)
md$community <- ifelse(lacto_frac >= 0.5, "lactobacillus", "anaerobe")

1. QC for this analysis

stopifnot(identical(colnames(sp), md$sample_id))  # order check: a silent
                                                  # mismatch would ruin everything
knitr::kable(table(Arm = md$arm, `RNA-seq batch` = md$rnaseq_batch),
             caption = "Samples per arm and sequencing batch")
Samples per arm and sequencing batch
B1 B2
injectable 20 19
pill 14 14
ring 13 13
  • Order check passed: species-table columns and metadata rows are in the same sample_id order.
  • Sample sizes: 28 pill, 39 injectable, 26 ring (93 total). The ring arm is the smallest, so ring comparisons carry the least power.
  • Carried flags from 01-qc.html: nine samples sit below half the median microbiome library size (lowest B006 at 5,247 reads); B030 is 99.8 % Lactobacillus iners (real biology, but it can pull ordinations); B018 and B029 lack cytokines (irrelevant here). None is dropped — the ordination in section 2 is the check that no flagged sample sits wildly alone.

2. Ordination: do the three arms separate?

We transform to CLR (centred log-ratio — each species compared against the geometric mean of the sample, the standard way to handle compositional data) and draw a Euclidean PCoA. Points are coloured by arm; the right panel reminds us what the big structure in this table actually is: community type, not method.

ps <- as_counts(dataset = "group_b", table = "microbiome", data = d)
sd <- as(sample_data(ps), "data.frame")
idx <- match(sd$sample_id, md$sample_id)
sd$arm       <- md$arm[idx]
sd$community <- md$community[idx]
sample_data(ps) <- sample_data(sd)

ord <- ps |>
  tax_transform("clr", zero_replace = "halfmin") |>
  dist_calc("euclidean") |>
  ord_calc("PCoA")

eig <- attr(ord, "ord")$CA$eig
sh  <- round(100 * eig / sum(eig), 1)

p_arm <- ord_plot(ord, axes = 1:2, color = "arm") +
  stat_ellipse(aes(colour = arm), type = "norm", linewidth = 0.4) +
  labs(title = "By method", x = sprintf("Axis 1 (%s%%)", sh[1]),
       y = sprintf("Axis 2 (%s%%)", sh[2]), colour = "Arm")
p_com <- ord_plot(ord, axes = 1:2, color = "community") +
  stat_ellipse(aes(colour = community), type = "norm", linewidth = 0.4) +
  labs(title = "By community type", x = sprintf("Axis 1 (%s%%)", sh[1]),
       y = NULL, colour = "Community")
p_arm + p_com

No sample sits in obvious isolation, so none of the flagged low-depth samples needs dropping.

3. PERMANOVA: a formal test of the map

PERMANOVA asks whether samples from different arms are further apart, on average, than samples from the same arm, and gets a p-value by shuffling the arm labels 9,999 times. R² is the share of all the between-sample variation the arm explains. Batch is included in the same model with by = "margin" so each term gets its own adjusted test (Anderson 2001).

dm <- attr(ord, "dist")
meta_p <- data.frame(sample_data(ps))[rownames(as.matrix(dm)), ]
meta_p$arm <- factor(meta_p$arm, levels = c("ring", "pill", "injectable"))
set.seed(1)
main <- adonis2(dm ~ arm + rnaseq_batch, data = meta_p,
                permutations = 9999, by = "margin")
disp <- permutest(betadisper(dm, meta_p$arm), permutations = 9999)

pair <- function(a, b) {
  keep <- meta_p$arm %in% c(a, b)
  out  <- adonis2(as.dist(as.matrix(dm)[keep, keep]) ~ arm,
                  data = droplevels(meta_p[keep, ]), permutations = 9999)
  tibble(comparison = paste(a, "vs", b),
         n = sum(keep),
         `share of variation (%)` = round(100 * out$R2[1], 1),
         `p (raw)` = out$`Pr(>F)`[1])
}
pairs <- bind_rows(pair("ring", "pill"),
                   pair("ring", "injectable"),
                   pair("pill", "injectable")) |>
  mutate(`p (adjusted, BH)` = p.adjust(`p (raw)`, "BH"))

q1_r2  <- round(100 * main$R2[1], 1)   # row 1 = arm (margin test)
q1_p   <- round(main$`Pr(>F)`[1], 3)
q1_rp  <- round(pairs$`p (raw)`[2], 3)
q1_ra  <- round(pairs$`p (adjusted, BH)`[2], 3)
q1_sp2 <- pairs$`share of variation (%)`[2]
q1_dp  <- round(disp$tab$`Pr(>F)`[1], 2)
knitr::kable(
  tibble(
    test = c("arm (adjusted for batch)", "batch (adjusted for arm)",
             "spread check (betadisper)"),
    n = c(93, 93, 93),
    `share of variation (%)` = round(100 * c(main$R2[1], main$R2[2], NA), 1),
    p = round(c(main$`Pr(>F)`[1], main$`Pr(>F)`[2],
                disp$tab$`Pr(>F)`[1]), 3)
  ),
  caption = "PERMANOVA on species (CLR + Euclidean, 9,999 permutations)"
)
PERMANOVA on species (CLR + Euclidean, 9,999 permutations)
test n share of variation (%) p
arm (adjusted for batch) 93 2.8 0.175
batch (adjusted for arm) 93 0.8 0.614
spread check (betadisper) 93 NA 0.895 
knitr::kable(pairs |>
               mutate(`p (raw)` = round(`p (raw)`, 3),
                      `p (adjusted, BH)` = round(`p (adjusted, BH)`, 3)),
             caption = "Each pair of arms separately (9,999 permutations)")
Each pair of arms separately (9,999 permutations)
comparison n share of variation (%) p (raw) p (adjusted, BH)
ring vs pill 54 1.7 0.445 0.445
ring vs injectable 65 1.7 0.309 0.445
pill vs injectable 67 2.7 0.084 0.251
  • Main test: the three arms explain 2.8 % of the species-level variation, p = 0.175 (n = 93). Not significant.
  • Pairwise: no pair survives adjustment; the largest raw effect is ring vs injectable at 1.7 % (raw p = 0.309, adjusted 0.445).
  • Spread check: the arms do not differ in how scattered they are (p = 0.89), so PERMANOVA is not being fooled by a difference in spread.

Sanity check. Change set.seed(1) to another number and re-render — the R² must stay exactly 2.8 % and the p-value should stay near 0.175. You can also verify the R² by hand: it is the between-arm sum of squares divided by the total, both printed by adonis2.

4. Differential abundance: do any individual species differ?

The ordination tests the whole profile at once; small shifts in a few species could still hide inside a non-significant map. DESeq2 tests each species separately. It takes raw counts (it does its own normalisation — never CPM or logged values) and, like the ordination, gets batch as a covariate. We first ask “does any arm differ?” with a likelihood-ratio test, then look at each pair.

sp_f <- sp[rowSums(sp >= 10) >= 10, ]    # same filter rule as the gene analyses
dds <- DESeq(DESeqDataSetFromMatrix(sp_f, md, design = ~ rnaseq_batch + arm),
             quiet = TRUE)
lrt <- as.data.frame(results(DESeq(DESeqDataSetFromMatrix(sp_f, md, ~ rnaseq_batch + arm),
                                   test = "LRT", reduced = ~ rnaseq_batch,
                                   quiet = TRUE))) |>
  rownames_to_column("taxon") |>
  left_join(d$taxonomy |> select(taxon, Genus, species), by = "taxon") |>
  mutate(padj = replace_na(padj, 1))

pair_res <- function(a, b) {
  as.data.frame(results(dds, contrast = c("arm", a, b))) |>
    rownames_to_column("taxon") |>
    left_join(d$taxonomy |> select(taxon, Genus, species), by = "taxon") |>
    mutate(padj = replace_na(padj, 1))
}
ring_pill <- pair_res("ring", "pill")
ring_inj  <- pair_res("ring", "injectable")
pill_inj  <- pair_res("pill", "injectable")
expected <- function(r) round(0.05 * sum(!is.na(r$pvalue)))
knitr::kable(
  tibble(
    comparison = c("any arm differs (LRT)", "ring vs pill", "ring vs injectable",
                   "pill vs injectable"),
    samples = c("93", "26 vs 28", "26 vs 39", "28 vs 39"),
    `species at FDR < 0.05` = c(sum(lrt$padj < 0.05),
                                sum(ring_pill$padj < 0.05),
                                sum(ring_inj$padj < 0.05),
                                sum(pill_inj$padj < 0.05)),
    `raw p < 0.05` = c(sum(lrt$pvalue < 0.05, na.rm = TRUE),
                       sum(ring_pill$pvalue < 0.05, na.rm = TRUE),
                       sum(ring_inj$pvalue < 0.05, na.rm = TRUE),
                       sum(pill_inj$pvalue < 0.05, na.rm = TRUE)),
    `expected by chance` = c(expected(lrt), expected(ring_pill),
                             expected(ring_inj), expected(pill_inj))
  ),
  caption = "DESeq2 on species (raw counts, batch-adjusted)"
)
DESeq2 on species (raw counts, batch-adjusted)
comparison samples species at FDR < 0.05 raw p < 0.05 expected by chance
any arm differs (LRT) 93 1 5 2
ring vs pill 26 vs 28 0 5 2
ring vs injectable 26 vs 39 3 5 2
pill vs injectable 28 vs 39 6 9 2 
top <- lrt |> filter(padj < 0.05) |>
  slice_min(padj, n = 10) |>
  transmute(species = str_c(Genus, " ", species),
            FDR = signif(padj, 2))
knitr::kable(top, caption = "Smallest-FDR species in the any-arm test")
Smallest-FDR species in the any-arm test
species FDR
Candidatus Lachnocurva Candidatus Lachnocurva_vaginae (BVAB1) 8.6e-05
  • The hit counts sit at or below what chance alone would give (220 species tested → about 11 expected at raw p < 0.05). Whatever small shifts exist are not concentrated in particular species.
  • One caveat that always applies here: these tables are compositional — “higher relative abundance” is not the same claim as “there was more of it”.

Sanity check. Pick the top species in the table, take its raw counts from 02_microbiome_counts.csv, and compare the ring-arm median with the pill-arm median by eye — a striking visual gap should match a small FDR, and here you should see mostly overlapping clouds, consistent with the non-significant tests.

5. Verdict

  • The three methods do not differ detectably in community composition. Ordination: no visible separation (n = 93). PERMANOVA: 2.8 %, p = 0.17; no pairwise comparison survives adjustment. DESeq2: hit counts at chance level, no species stands out.
  • The strong structure in this table is community type (48 lactobacillus-dominant vs 45 anaerobe samples, axis 1 = 36 %) — and community type is balanced across the arms, which is why the method comparison is not chasing it. Question 3 (06-q3-community-vs-method.html) follows that split into the genes.
  • With 26–39 people per arm, a real but modest effect could still hide here; absence of evidence, not evidence of absence.

Choices made

  • CLR + Euclidean for the ordination and PERMANOVA, because species profiles are compositional; Bray-Curtis on raw counts and Jaccard on presence/absence were the alternatives and give the same picture (see 01-qc.html, section 9).
  • Species table left unfiltered for the ordination, matching 01-qc.html; the DESeq2 abundance test filters at ≥ 10 reads in ≥ 10 samples, the same rule as the gene analyses — a laxer rule spends tests on near-empty species, a stricter one loses power.
  • PERMANOVA with batch in one model, by = "margin", 9,999 permutations — the correction from 03-three-arms-review.html; the default sequential test gives the first term credit for anything it shares with the second. The batch label is the RNA-seq run, the only batch information the metadata carries; if the microbiome was sequenced in different runs, that variable is not available to adjust for.
  • Likelihood-ratio test for “does any arm differ?” (2 df) before any pairwise look; jumping straight to pairwise tests is the alternative and invites cherry-picking.
  • BH adjustment for the pairwise PERMANOVA p-values; Bonferroni is the stricter alternative.
  • Kept all 93 samples, including the nine low-depth ones and the B030 near-monoculture; dropping them is the alternative but none drives the (null) result, and CLR with half-min replacement handles the zeros.
  • Did not adjust for vaginal pH here — pH differs by arm (p = 0.02) and could be on the causal path from hormones to microbiome; an adjusted model is the alternative and belongs in a follow-up rather than a null-result document.
